digestion.title: Follow a bite of food
digestion.summary: Watch one bite travel from the mouth to the end of the gut and see what each organ does to it along the way.

mouth.title: Chewing and saliva
mouth.body: Teeth cut and grind the bite while the tongue rolls it around. Three pairs of salivary glands add saliva, which wets the food so it can be swallowed and carries amylase, an enzyme that starts breaking starch into sugars. The softened lump is called a bolus.

swallow.title: The swallow
swallow.body: The tongue pushes the bolus back into the throat (pharynx). The soft palate and uvula lift to seal off the nose, and the epiglottis, a leaf-shaped flap, folds down over the windpipe so food goes into the esophagus instead of the lungs. Throat muscles squeeze it downward.

esophagus.title: Down the esophagus
esophagus.body: Waves of muscle contraction called peristalsis squeeze the bolus down this 25 cm tube in a few seconds. They work even if you are upside down. At the bottom, a ring of muscle opens to let food into the stomach and closes again to keep acid out.

stomach.title: Churning in the stomach
stomach.body: The stomach's muscular walls churn the food with gastric juice: hydrochloric acid and pepsin, an enzyme that starts breaking proteins apart. After a few hours the food has become chyme, a thick acidic liquid, and is let out a little at a time through the pylorus.

duodenum.title: Juices join in the duodenum
duodenum.body: In the first part of the small intestine, bile made by the liver and stored in the gallbladder arrives through the bile duct and breaks fat into tiny droplets. The pancreas adds juice that neutralises the acid and carries enzymes for carbohydrates, proteins and fats.

small-intestine.title: Absorbing in the small intestine
small-intestine.body: Along several metres of coiled intestine, enzymes finish breaking food into its smallest pieces: sugars, amino acids and fatty acids. Millions of tiny finger-like folds called villi absorb them into the blood and lymph. This model shows the jejunum and ileum together as one coil.

large-intestine.title: Water and bacteria in the large intestine
large-intestine.body: What's left, mostly fibre and water, enters the large intestine near the appendix and travels up, across and down the colon. The colon absorbs most of the remaining water and salts, and trillions of gut bacteria ferment fibre the body couldn't digest. The leftovers become stool.

exit.title: Out of the body
exit.body: Stool is stored in the rectum until the body is ready to empty it, then leaves through the anal canal, controlled by ring-shaped sphincter muscles.
exit.note: The rectum and anal canal aren't in the 3D model yet, so the route is dashed here.

blood.title: Follow a drop of blood
blood.summary: Ride one drop of blood from your left hand to the heart, through the lungs, and back again. The full trip takes about a minute at rest.
blood.metersNote: Typical resting values; carbon dioxide on a relative scale.

hand.title: Delivering oxygen in the hand
hand.body: In the hand, arteries branch into capillaries thinner than a hair. Here the blood hands oxygen and nutrients to the cells and picks up carbon dioxide, their waste gas. Oxygen-poor blood is darker red; it only looks blue through the skin.
hand.note: Capillaries are too small to be in the 3D model, so the route is dashed here.

arm-veins.title: Up the arm in the veins
arm-veins.body: Veins collect the blood and carry it back toward the heart. The pressure here is low, so one-way valves inside the veins stop blood from sliding back, and the squeeze of the arm muscles helps push it along.

to-heart.title: Into the great veins
to-heart.body: The arm vein joins veins from the head and neck. On the left they form the brachiocephalic vein, which crosses the chest to join the superior vena cava, the large vein that empties blood from the upper body into the heart's right atrium.

right-heart.title: Through the right side of the heart
right-heart.body: From the right atrium the blood passes the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. When the ventricle squeezes, the valve snaps shut and the blood is pushed through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk, toward the lungs.

to-lungs.title: Off to the lungs
to-lungs.body: The pulmonary trunk splits into a right and a left pulmonary artery. These are the only arteries that carry oxygen-poor blood, which is why diagrams often colour them blue. This drop takes the left branch into the left lung.

lung-capillaries.title: Picking up oxygen
lung-capillaries.body: In the lungs the arteries branch into capillaries wrapped around millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli. Oxygen moves from the air into the blood and binds to red blood cells, while carbon dioxide moves out to be breathed away. The blood turns bright red.
lung-capillaries.note: The lung capillaries and air sacs are too small for the 3D model; the close-up shows what happens.

back-to-heart.title: Back to the heart
back-to-heart.body: Oxygen-rich blood leaves the lung through the pulmonary veins, the only veins that carry oxygen-rich blood, and flows into the left atrium.

left-heart.title: Through the left side of the heart
left-heart.body: The blood passes the mitral valve into the left ventricle, the heart's strongest chamber, whose thick wall pumps blood to the whole body. Each squeeze pushes it through the aortic valve into the aorta. Just above the valve, the coronary arteries branch off to feed the heart muscle itself.

aorta.title: The aorta
aorta.body: The aorta, the body's largest artery, rises from the heart and curves over in the aortic arch. Branches from the arch supply the head and arms; this drop turns into the left subclavian artery, heading for the left arm.

arm-arteries.title: Down the arm to the hand
arm-arteries.body: Arteries carry the blood down the arm: the axillary artery in the armpit, the brachial artery in the upper arm, then the radial artery on the thumb side of the forearm, where you can feel your pulse at the wrist. Then it is back to the hand's capillaries, and the loop starts again.

breath.title: Follow a breath of air
breath.summary: Breathe in with one breath of air through the nose and down the windpipe to the lungs' tiny air sacs, then back out again.

nose.title: In through the nose
nose.body: Air enters through the nostrils into the nasal cavity. Hairs and sticky mucus trap dust, and curled bony shelves called conchae swirl the air over a warm, moist lining, so it reaches the lungs warmed, humidified and cleaner.

throat.title: Down the throat
throat.body: Behind the nose the air passes into the pharynx, the throat space shared with food. While you breathe, the soft palate hangs down and the epiglottis stands open, leaving the way into the voice box clear.

larynx.title: Through the voice box
larynx.body: The larynx, or voice box, is a frame of cartilages, including the thyroid cartilage that forms the Adam's apple. Air passes between the vocal folds inside it; when they are pulled together and vibrate, they make the sound of your voice.

trachea.title: Down the windpipe
trachea.body: The trachea is a tube about 10 to 12 cm long held open by C-shaped rings of cartilage. Its lining is covered in tiny hairs called cilia that sweep mucus and trapped dust up toward the throat, away from the lungs.

bronchi.title: Branching into the bronchi
bronchi.body: The trachea splits into two main bronchi. The right one is wider, shorter and steeper, so this breath follows it, then branches again toward the lower lobe of the right lung. The airways keep dividing, more than 20 times, into ever smaller tubes.

alveoli.title: Swapping gases in the air sacs
alveoli.body: The smallest airways end in clusters of alveoli, hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs with walls thinner than a cell. Oxygen crosses into the blood in the surrounding capillaries, and carbon dioxide crosses the other way into the air.
alveoli.note: Alveoli are far too small for the 3D model; the close-up shows what happens.

breathe-out.title: Breathing out
breathe-out.body: The diaphragm, the dome-shaped muscle under the lungs, relaxes and rises, and the stretchy lungs spring back. That pushes the used air back up through the bronchi, the trachea and the voice box. Breathing out at rest takes no muscle effort at all.

out-nose.title: Out through the nose
out-nose.body: The air leaves with less oxygen and about a hundred times more carbon dioxide than it came in with. At rest you repeat this about 12 to 20 times a minute, moving about half a litre of air each breath.
